summaries.example: Imagine you promised to help two friends at the same time. Both need you, but you can reach only one. Helping either friend seems right, and refusing both seems wrong. This is a moral conflict. Philosophers ask whether it is a true dilemma or whether one duty should count as more important.
summaries.summary: A moral dilemma is a hard situation in which someone seems required to do two things, can do each one, but cannot do both. Philosophers disagree about whether these are genuine moral dilemmas. Some say one duty must always win, or that the person has a choice between equally acceptable actions. Others think that sometimes every available choice involves moral loss. The entry also explains why rules, emotions, and ideas about what people can do matter in this debate.
key_ideas: Moral dilemmas involve duties that point in different directions.
A conflict is not always a true dilemma. One duty may be more important and settle the choice.
Some philosophers think genuine dilemmas exist; others think every case can be resolved.
Feeling regret after a choice does not always prove that the person did something wrong.
summaries.why_it_matters: Real life can involve promises, friendships, family responsibilities, jobs, and duties to strangers. Thinking about moral dilemmas helps us explain why a choice is difficult instead of simply calling someone good or bad. It also reminds us to separate not knowing the right answer from there being no single right answer.

important_terms.definition: A situation in which a person seems required to do two actions but cannot do both.
A rule or reason about what someone should or should not do.
A conflict in which one duty is judged more important than another.
A painful feeling that may remain after a difficult moral choice.

questions_to_think_about: Can two good duties ever be impossible to follow together?
If you must choose between helping two people, what would make one choice better?
Is regret the same as guilt? Why or why not?

summaries.example: A defense attorney may have a duty to protect information shared by a client and a duty to be truthful before a court. If these duties conflict, one response is to say that confidentiality or honesty takes priority in the circumstances. A supporter of genuine dilemmas might argue that neither duty is overridden. The example therefore illustrates the difference between an unresolved conflict in practice and an ontological dilemma, where neither requirement is actually stronger.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether genuine moral dilemmas are possible. A genuine dilemma requires more than an unpleasant choice: an agent must have two obligations, be able to fulfill each separately, be unable to fulfill both, and face requirements that are equally binding rather than ranked by priority. Critics argue that dilemmas conflict with principles used in deontic logic, including the claim that obligations cannot require both an act and its denial, that ought implies can, and that separate obligations combine into a single obligation. Supporters can challenge these principles or argue that moral requirements sometimes resist ranking. The discussion also considers moral residue, the difference between guilt and regret, several types of dilemmas, conflicts between general and role-related duties, and disagreements among multiple moral frameworks.
key_ideas: The central issue is not merely conflict, but conflict between requirements that are both feasible separately and neither of which overrides the other.
Opponents of dilemmas often appeal to principles such as deontic consistency, ought implies can, or the idea that combined obligations can be fulfilled together.
Defenders of dilemmas may reject one of those principles, or argue that some requirements cannot be ranked or compensated for.
Moral guilt and remorse can support the dilemma view, but critics distinguish them from regret and argue that negative emotions can be appropriate even when no wrongdoing occurred.
The entry distinguishes epistemic from ontological conflicts, self-imposed from externally imposed dilemmas, and obligation from prohibition dilemmas.
General duties and role-based duties can conflict, raising questions about how different parts of morality fit together.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests what moral theories are supposed to do. If morality guides action, should it always identify a single permissible path? If a person must violate one important requirement, should that person be judged blameworthy, regretful, or both? These questions matter in personal choices and in professional, legal, medical, and political roles. They also show why examples alone do not settle philosophical disputes: each side must explain both the cases and the principles used to interpret them.

important_terms.definition: A case in which an agent is required to perform each of two or more actions, can perform each separately, but cannot perform them all together, with neither requirement overriding the other.
A conflict in which the agent does not know which requirement has priority, although one requirement may in fact be stronger.
A conflict in which neither competing requirement is stronger or cancels the other.
The claim that if an action is morally required, it must be possible for the agent to perform it.
The principle that being obligated to do A and obligated to do B entails being obligated to do both A and B.
The leftover guilt, remorse, regret, apology, or compensation that may follow a morally serious choice.
A moral theory is action-guiding when it classifies options as forbidden, permissible, or obligatory; it is uniquely action-guiding when it does not recommend incompatible actions or leave a gap.

questions_to_think_about: Does uncertainty about consequences show that a dilemma is genuine, or only that the agent lacks information?
Should a moral theory always provide one permissible course of action?
Can regret be appropriate without guilt? What does that imply about moral residue?
Are duties created by a professional role fundamentally different from general moral duties?
Is choosing one of two equally worthy options a moral failure, or a disjunctive way of fulfilling one duty?

summaries.example: Suppose Maya agrees to help her younger brother prepare for an important performance. On the same afternoon, she promises a new student that she will guide them through a difficult school project. Maya can help either person well, but not both. One philosopher might say helping her brother matters more because of their relationship. Another might say the duties are equally serious, so Maya faces a real dilemma. A third might say she should help one or the other, and that choosing either satisfies a broader duty to help someone.
summaries.summary: Moral dilemmas are cases in which a person seems to have two obligations that cannot both be fulfilled. Philosophers disagree about whether such cases are genuine. One side says that a good moral theory must avoid requiring impossible combinations or incompatible actions. The other side says that some obligations may be equally strong, so no ranking can remove the conflict. The entry separates real conflicts from uncertainty, examines guilt and regret after difficult choices, and classifies dilemmas in several ways. It also asks how ordinary moral duties connect with duties created by jobs, relationships, or public roles.
key_ideas: Not every moral conflict is a genuine dilemma. If one duty overrides another, the case may be difficult but settled.
Some philosophers reject dilemmas because moral theories should give consistent and useful guidance.
Others argue that certain cases remain balanced even after all relevant facts are considered.
Moral feelings after a choice are important evidence for the debate, but guilt and regret do not mean exactly the same thing.
Dilemmas can be self-created, imposed by circumstances, involve one person or several, and concern required actions or forbidden actions.
Different kinds of obligations, including general duties and role-related duties, may point toward different choices.
summaries.why_it_matters: Moral decisions are not always simple rule-following exercises. A person may have responsibilities to family, friends, strangers, an institution, or a professional role. Studying dilemmas helps us ask whether a difficult choice means someone did wrong, whether the situation itself was unfair, and whether moral theories can guide people when important values collide.

important_terms.definition: A situation where a person has two moral duties, can carry out each one alone, but cannot carry out both.
A conflict where one moral rule or duty has priority over another in the situation.
A conflict caused by not knowing which duty is stronger, even though one may actually be stronger.
A conflict where neither duty has priority, rather than merely seeming equal because of uncertainty.
The idea that a person cannot be morally required to do what is beyond their power.
The idea that two separate obligations can be combined into an obligation to do both.
A lingering moral response, such as guilt, regret, apology, or a need to make amends, after a difficult choice.
A duty connected to a job, social position, or relationship, such as a lawyer’s duty of confidentiality.

questions_to_think_about: What evidence would show that one duty overrides another?
Is a choice still a dilemma if the person simply does not know enough facts?
Why might someone regret an outcome without believing they acted wrongly?
Should a person be held responsible for a conflict they created by making two incompatible promises?
Can a rule that works well in ordinary cases create trouble in an unusual case?
